facts.fact: The Rigveda mentions Sabha, Samiti and Vidatha as local bodies.
The Shanti Parva, the Manusmriti and the Arthashastra describe village self-rule.
The Mahabharata names the Gramik, Dashap, Vinshya Adhipati, Shat Gram Adhyaksha and Shat Gram Pati.
In the Gupta period the district official was the Vishaya Pati and the village headman the Grampati.
Sultanate villages had the Mukkaddam, Patwari and Choudhri.
Lord Mayo's Resolution of 1870 began financial decentralisation.
Lord Ripon's 1882 Resolution is the Magna Carta of local self-government; Ripon is its father.
The Royal Commission on Decentralisation (1907) was chaired by C.E.H. Hobhouse.
The Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (1919) made local government a transferred provincial subject.
By 1925 eight provinces and six princely states had passed Panchayat Acts.
Article 40 (a DPSP) asks the state to organise village panchayats; Ambedkar was sceptical.
The CDP began on 2 October 1952, inspired by Albert Mayer's Etawah project; the NES followed in 1953.
The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957), set up by the NDC, recommended three tiers and democratic decentralisation.
Balwant Rai Mehta made the samiti executive, the zilla parishad advisory and the Collector its chairman.
The NDC accepted the Balwant Rai Mehta report in January 1958.
Rajasthan inaugurated Panchayati Raj at Nagaur on 2 October 1959 (Nehru); AP followed on 1 November 1959.
The Ashok Mehta Committee (1977) recommended two tiers — zilla parishad and mandal panchayat.
Ashok Mehta proposed mandals of 15,000-20,000 people and open participation of political parties.
The G.V.K. Rao Committee (1985) called PRIs "grass without roots" and made the district the planning unit.
The L.M. Singhvi Committee (1986) recommended constitutional recognition for PRIs.
The P.K. Thungon Committee (1988) made the zilla parishad the pivot with the Collector as chief executive.
The Gadgil Committee (1988) proposed reservations and State Finance and Election Commissions.
The 64th Amendment Bill (1989) under Rajiv Gandhi failed in the Rajya Sabha.
The Narasimha Rao government's bill became the 73rd Amendment, in force on 24 April 1993, National Panchayati Raj Day.
The Ministry of Panchayati Raj was created in 2004.
The 2nd ARC sixth report, "Local Governance — An Inspiring Journey into the Future", urged subsidiarity and activity mapping.
The 73rd and 74th Amendments created what is called multi-level federalism.
Article 243A: the Gram Sabha consists of all persons on the village electoral roll; powers as state law provides.
Article 243B: three tiers; the intermediate tier may be skipped in states of not more than 20 lakh.
Article 243C: all seats by direct election; intermediate and district chairpersons elected indirectly.
Article 243D reserves seats for SCs/STs by population and not less than one-third for women, including SC/ST women.
Chairperson posts are reserved for SCs, STs and women by rotation; backward-class reservation is optional.
Article 243E: five-year term; election within six months of dissolution; remainder of term after premature dissolution (UPSC 2016).
The minimum age for a panchayat seat is 21, not 25 (Art 243F; UPSC 2016).
Article 243G: panchayats prepare plans for economic development and social justice (UPSC 2013).
Article 243H: panchayats levy taxes only as the state legislature authorises.
Article 243I: the Governor constitutes a State Finance Commission every five years.
Article 243J covers audit of panchayat accounts.
Article 243K: the State Election Commissioner is appointed by the Governor and removed only like an HC judge.
Article 243L applies Part IX to UTs as the President directs.
Article 243M exempts Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Scheduled and tribal areas, Manipur hill areas and Darjeeling.
Article 243N continues existing panchayat laws for one year.
Article 243O bars courts in panchayat electoral matters except by election petition.
The 73rd Amendment added Art 280(3)(bb) on Finance Commission measures for panchayats.
Representation of MPs and MLAs in panchayats is a voluntary provision.
Compulsory provisions include the Gram Sabha, three tiers, direct elections, women's reservation, the SEC and the SFC.
Financial powers to levy taxes and devolution of Eleventh Schedule subjects are voluntary.
Agriculture, land reforms, minor irrigation, animal husbandry, fisheries and social forestry are Eleventh Schedule items.
Minor forest produce, khadi and village industries, rural housing and drinking water are Eleventh Schedule items.
Fuel and fodder, ferries, rural electrification and non-conventional energy are Eleventh Schedule items.
Education including primary and secondary schools, vocational education, adult education and libraries are Eleventh Schedule items.
Cultural activities, markets and fairs, health and sanitation and family welfare are Eleventh Schedule items.
Women and child development, weaker sections, the PDS and maintenance of community assets are Eleventh Schedule items.
Urban planning, land use regulation, roads and bridges and water supply are Twelfth Schedule items.
Fire services, urban forestry, slum improvement and urban poverty alleviation are Twelfth Schedule items.
Burials and cremation grounds, cattle pounds, vital statistics and slaughter houses are Twelfth Schedule items.
Solid waste management, parks and playgrounds and street lighting are Twelfth Schedule items.
Drinking water is in the Eleventh Schedule; water supply for domestic, industrial and commercial use in the Twelfth.
PESA was passed on the Dilip Singh Bhuria Committee's advice and came into force on 24 December 1996.
PESA covers ten states including Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.
Under PESA the Gram Sabha is consulted before land acquisition and owns minor forest produce.
Under PESA the Gram Sabha controls money-lending, can prohibit intoxicants and recommends minor mineral leases.
PESA reserves at least half the seats and all chairperson posts for STs.
Creating autonomous regions is not an objective of PESA (UPSC 2013).
Andhra Pradesh framed PESA Rules in 2011; the nodal ministry is Panchayati Raj.
Article 243Q: Nagar Panchayat, Municipal Council, Municipal Corporation, classified by the Governor.
The Governor uses population, density, revenue and non-agricultural employment; industrial townships may be exempted.
Article 243R lets persons with municipal experience sit without a vote.
Article 243S requires Wards Committees where population is three lakh or more.
Article 243T reserves seats; Article 243U gives a five-year term.
Article 243W gives powers including Twelfth Schedule subjects; 243X taxes.
Article 243Y: the SFC reviews municipal finances; 243ZA: the SEC conducts municipal polls.
Article 243ZC exempts Scheduled and tribal areas and the Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council area.
At least four-fifths of a District Planning Committee (243ZD) are elected from the district panchayat and municipal members.
A Metropolitan Planning Committee (243ZE) is for 10 lakh or more, with two-thirds elected.
Article 243ZG bars courts in municipal electoral matters.
All members of a Notified Area Committee are nominated by the state government.
A Town Area Committee governs a small town with limited functions.
Cantonment Boards work under the Ministry of Defence and the Cantonments Act 2006.
A township has no elected members; port trusts and special purpose agencies are other urban bodies.
Bombay and Calcutta got municipal corporations in 1726, after Madras (1688).
The 65th Amendment (Nagarpalika) Bill, 1989 failed; the 74th came into force on 1 June 1993.
Urban local bodies come under the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs.
The Constitution fixes no population cut-offs for the three types of municipality.
AP adopted Panchayati Raj under the AP Panchayat Samithis and Zilla Parishads Act, 1959.
The N.T. Rama Rao government created mandals in 1985-86, inspired by the Ashok Mehta Committee.
Mandal Praja Parishads were set up under a 1986 Act.
The AP Panchayat Raj Act, 1994 (Act 13 of 1994) gave effect to the 73rd Amendment.
In AP the Sarpanch is directly elected, the MPP President by MPTCs and the ZPP Chairperson by ZPTCs.
AP reserves 50% of local-body seats for women.
AP urban bodies work mainly under the AP Municipalities Act, 1965.
Deputy CM Konidela Pawan Kalyan holds the Panchayat Raj and Rural Development portfolio.
AP's Grama and Ward Sachivalayams began on 2 October 2019 — about 15,004 Grama and 3,842 Ward Sachivalayams.
The secretariats are now called Swarna Grama and Swarna Ward Sachivalayams.
AP's 28 Zilla Praja Parishads came into effect on 25 September 2026.
SEC Anil Chandra Punetha announced AP's local-body poll schedule on 14 October 2026.
AP urban local body polls are on 28 October 2026 and MPTC/ZPTC polls on 3 November 2026.
AP gram panchayat polls are in three phases from 26 November to 2 December 2026.
The 73rd Amendment added Part IX (Arts 243-243O) and the Eleventh Schedule of 29 subjects.
The 74th Amendment added Part IXA (Arts 243P-243ZG) and the Twelfth Schedule of 18 subjects.
The Eleventh Schedule has 29 subjects and the Twelfth 18.
Ripon's Resolution of 1882 is the Magna Carta of local self-government.
Panchayat elections are run by the State Election Commission, not the Election Commission of India.
India's first municipal corporation was set up at Madras in 1688.
A Nagar Panchayat is for an area in transition from rural to urban.
PESA covers the Fifth Schedule, not the Sixth Schedule areas of the North-East.
SVAMITVA uses drones to survey abadi land and issue property cards; it is run by the Ministry of Panchayati Raj.
Effective decentralisation needs transfer of funds, functions and functionaries (the 3 Fs).
The Constitution does not make devolution of all 29 Eleventh Schedule subjects mandatory.
State Finance Commission recommendations are not binding on the state government.
In AP the intermediate tier is the Mandal Praja Parishad.
AP has had 28 districts since 31 December 2025, Polavaram and Markapuram being the newest.
AP secretariats are backed by volunteers and do not replace the constitutional Gram Sabha.
GVMC (Visakhapatnam) is among AP's largest municipal corporations.
